holding_as_summarised: Yes. The fee policy was a justified use of limited public resources.

name: GA and others v. Director of Immigration
court: Court of Final Appeal, Hong Kong
holding_as_summarised: No. The Basic Law’s freedom to choose an occupation does not extend to people without the right to take up employment; the Director keeps discretion to permit work.

name: Kong Yunming v. Director of Social Welfare
court: Court of Final Appeal, Hong Kong
holding_as_summarised: No. The requirement, raised from one year to seven in 2004, was unconstitutional; the one-year rule was restored.

name: Ng Ka Ling v. Director of Immigration
court: Court of Final Appeal, Hong Kong
flags: source is a portal or search page: link the judgment itself
holding_as_summarised: Yes. The right of abode in the Basic Law could not be made subject to a one-way permit scheme or limited to children born after a parent became a resident.

name: Ghulam Rbani v. Secretary for Justice
court: Court of Final Appeal, Hong Kong
flags: source is a portal or search page: link the judgment itself
holding_as_summarised: No. Detention requires an actual decision applying the published policy; without it, part of the detention was unlawful and damages were due.

name: Ubamaka v. Secretary for Security
court: Court of Final Appeal, Hong Kong
flags: source is a portal or search page: link the judgment itself
holding_as_summarised: No. The protection against cruel treatment is absolute and applies to removal, but the facts did not reach that level; the appeal was dismissed.

name: People’s Union for Democratic Rights v. Union of India (Asiad workers)
flags: source is a portal or search page: link the judgment itself
holding_as_summarised: Yes. Paying less than the minimum wage is forced labour under Article 23; the State must enforce labour laws against contractors.

name: Bandhua Mukti Morcha v. Union of India
flags: source is a portal or search page: link the judgment itself
holding_as_summarised: Yes. The Court issued detailed directions for release, rehabilitation and enforcement of labour laws.

name: Bachpan Bachao Andolan v. Union of India (children in circuses)
flags: source is a portal or search page: link the judgment itself
holding_as_summarised: Yes. Employing children in circuses was prohibited, raids and rescue were ordered, and the government had to act against trafficking.

name: Chairman, Railway Board v. Chandrima Das
flags: source is a portal or search page: link the judgment itself
holding_as_summarised: Yes. The right to life and dignity under Article 21 protects every person, citizen or not; the Railways were liable to pay compensation.

name: National Campaign Committee for Central Legislation on Construction Labour v. Union of India
flags: source is a portal or search page: link the judgment itself
holding_as_summarised: No. The Court found large sums unspent or misused and directed registration of workers and a model welfare scheme.

name: Louis De Raedt v. Union of India
flags: source is a portal or search page: link the judgment itself
holding_as_summarised: No. A foreigner’s right to life and liberty is protected, but the right to reside and settle is reserved to citizens; the power to expel is unlimited by the Constitution.

name: Neeraja Chaudhary v. State of Madhya Pradesh
flags: source is a portal or search page: link the judgment itself
holding_as_summarised: Release must be followed by rehabilitation; failing to rehabilitate freed bonded labourers breaches Article 21.

name: Labourers Working on Salal Hydro Project v. State of Jammu and Kashmir
flags: exact date missing; source is a portal or search page: link the judgment itself
holding_as_summarised: Yes. The Court directed enforcement, including against child labour on the site.

name: Mohammad Salimullah v. Union of India
flags: source is a portal or search page: link the judgment itself
holding_as_summarised: No interim relief. The court declined to halt deportation, saying it would follow the procedure for deportation; the main petition is pending.

name: Sarbananda Sonowal v. Union of India
flags: source is a portal or search page: link the judgment itself
holding_as_summarised: No. The Illegal Migrants (Determination by Tribunals) Act 1983 was struck down; the Foreigners Act, which puts the burden on the person to prove citizenship, applies in Assam.

name: Vishal Jeet v. Union of India
flags: source is a portal or search page: link the judgment itself
holding_as_summarised: The state must take strict action under the trafficking law and set up advisory committees and rehabilitation schemes.

name: Chong Hyang Gyun v. Tokyo Metropolitan Government
holding_as_summarised: Yes. Reserving posts that involve exercising public authority to nationals does not breach equality.

name: Lost earnings of an injured worker without a visa
flags: source is a portal or search page: link the judgment itself
holding_as_summarised: On Japanese wages for the period he could expect to stay, then on wages in his home country.

name: McLean v. Minister of Justice
holding_as_summarised: Yes. Constitutional rights extend to foreigners, but within the framework of the residence system; the Minister has broad discretion over renewals.

name: Nationality Act Article 3 case
holding_as_summarised: No. The marriage requirement in Article 3(1) breached equality under Article 14 of the Constitution.

name: Local voting rights of permanent residents
flags: source is a portal or search page: link the judgment itself
holding_as_summarised: No, but the Constitution does not forbid Parliament from granting it.

name: Permanent residents and public assistance
flags: source is a portal or search page: link the judgment itself
holding_as_summarised: No. The Act covers Japanese nationals; foreigners receive assistance only as an administrative measure, not as a legal entitlement.

name: Limits on changing workplace (second challenge)
flags: no official source linked
holding_as_summarised: No. The Court again upheld the limits.

name: Exclusion of farm workers from working-hours rules
flags: source is a portal or search page: link the judgment itself
holding_as_summarised: No. The exclusion in Article 63 was upheld.

name: Undocumented worker and industrial accident compensation
flags: source is a portal or search page: link the judgment itself
holding_as_summarised: Yes. A contract with a worker who lacks work authorisation is not void for that reason, and the injured worker is a “worker” entitled to benefits.

name: Seoul-Gyeonggi-Incheon Migrants’ Trade Union v. Minister of Labor
holding_as_summarised: Yes. Anyone who lives on wages from work is a worker under the Trade Union Act, whatever their immigration status; refusing the union’s registration on that ground was unlawful.

name: Severance pay paid only after departure
flags: no official source linked
holding_as_summarised: Yes. The Court found the rule, meant to discourage overstaying, constitutional.

name: Industrial trainees and the Labor Standards Act
flags: no official source linked
holding_as_summarised: No. Excluding them from protections such as paid leave and overtime pay breached equality.

name: Lubiano v. Director of Immigration
holding_as_summarised: Yes. The Director of Immigration may impose the live-in condition; the Court of Appeal held it falls within Hong Kong’s reservation to Article 6 of the ICESCR and does not itself force helpers to work on rest days.

name: Decision 127/PUU-XXI/2023 (fishing crew under the migrant worker protection law)
holding_as_summarised: The Court rejected the petition. Ship crew and fishers working abroad remain migrant workers covered by the protection law (Art. 4(1)(c)).

name: Datuman v. First Cosmopolitan Manpower
holding_as_summarised: Yes. Contract substitution is prohibited and the agency is jointly liable for the difference.

name: JMM Promotion and Management v. Court of Appeals
holding_as_summarised: Yes. The requirement was a reasonable protective regulation.

name: People v. Lalli
flags: source is a portal or search page: link the judgment itself
holding_as_summarised: Yes. The convictions for trafficking in persons and illegal recruitment were upheld.

name: Macalintal v. Commission on Elections (overseas absentee voting)
flags: source is a portal or search page: link the judgment itself
holding_as_summarised: Yes. The Overseas Absentee Voting Act was largely upheld; Filipinos abroad keep their domicile at home for voting purposes. Some provisions giving Congress oversight of the election body were struck down.

name: Philippine Association of Service Exporters v. Drilon
holding_as_summarised: Yes. The deployment ban was a valid exercise of police power and did not breach equal protection.

name: Sto. Tomas v. Salac
flags: source is a portal or search page: link the judgment itself
holding_as_summarised: Yes. Joint and several liability of corporate officers serves the state’s duty to protect overseas workers.

name: PERT/CPM Manpower Exponent Co. v. Vinuya
flags: source is a portal or search page: link the judgment itself
holding_as_summarised: Yes. Substituting worse contracts amounted to constructive dismissal, and the recruitment agency was jointly liable for the workers’ money claims.

name: Yap v. Thenamaris Ship’s Management
flags: source is a portal or search page: link the judgment itself
holding_as_summarised: Yes. Following Serrano, the three-month cap was unconstitutional and the seafarer was owed salary for the unexpired portion of his contract.

name: Darshan Masih v. The State (brick kiln workers)
flags: exact date missing; source is a portal or search page: link the judgment itself
holding_as_summarised: Yes. The Court held bonded labour unconstitutional and gave interim directions; Parliament later passed the Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act 1992.

name: Serrano v. Gallant Maritime Services
holding_as_summarised: The cap in Section 10 of Republic Act 8042 was struck down as a breach of equal protection; the worker was owed his salary for the whole unexpired term.

name: Public Prosecutor v. Gaiyathiri d/o Murugayan
holding_as_summarised: Life imprisonment, after she pleaded guilty to culpable homicide and other charges.

name: J.Y. Interpretation No. 497 (entry and residence of people from mainland China)
holding_as_summarised: Yes. The restrictions were authorised by statute and did not breach freedom of residence and movement.

name: J.Y. Interpretation No. 618 (former mainland spouses and public office)
holding_as_summarised: Yes. The ten-year wait was a reasonable distinction and did not breach equality.

name: J.Y. Interpretation No. 710 (deportation and detention of mainland Chinese residents)
holding_as_summarised: Yes. Removal must allow a chance to be heard, and detention pending removal must be limited and subject to prompt judicial review.

name: Vallejos v. Commissioner of Registration
court: Court of Final Appeal, Hong Kong
holding_as_summarised: Yes. Given the nature of helpers’ residence (tied to a specific employer and contract, with return expected), the exclusion is consistent with Article 24(2)(4) of the Basic Law.

name: C.N. v. the United Kingdom
holding_as_summarised: No. Without a specific offence the investigation could not be effective; violation of Article 4.

name: Andrejeva v. Latvia (Grand Chamber)
flags: source is a portal or search page: link the judgment itself
holding_as_summarised: No. The difference in treatment based on nationality lacked an objective and reasonable justification.

name: Čonka v. Belgium
flags: source is a portal or search page: link the judgment itself
holding_as_summarised: No. The arrest by a misleading summons breached liberty, and the removal was a collective expulsion without an effective remedy.

name: Gaygusuz v. Austria
flags: source is a portal or search page: link the judgment itself
holding_as_summarised: No. Only very weighty reasons could justify a difference based on nationality; the refusal breached Article 14 with Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

name: Hirsi Jamaa v. Italy (Grand Chamber)
flags: source is a portal or search page: link the judgment itself
holding_as_summarised: No. The pushback exposed them to ill-treatment, amounted to collective expulsion, and denied an effective remedy.

name: J. and Others v. Austria
flags: source is a portal or search page: link the judgment itself
holding_as_summarised: No. Austria identified the women as possible victims and protected them in Austria; Article 4 did not require it to investigate acts committed abroad.

name: Jeunesse v. the Netherlands (Grand Chamber)
flags: source is a portal or search page: link the judgment itself
holding_as_summarised: Yes, in the circumstances. Refusing her residence failed to give enough weight to the best interests of the children.

name: Khlaifia v. Italy (Grand Chamber)
flags: source is a portal or search page: link the judgment itself
holding_as_summarised: The detention lacked a legal basis and judicial review (Article 5 violated), but there was no collective expulsion because each received an individual identification.

name: Koua Poirrez v. France
flags: source is a portal or search page: link the judgment itself
holding_as_summarised: No. Refusing the allowance on grounds of nationality breached Article 14 with Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

name: Kurić v. Slovenia (Grand Chamber)
flags: source is a portal or search page: link the judgment itself
holding_as_summarised: Yes. The “erasure” breached private and family life and equality, and the state had to set up a compensation scheme.

name: Paposhvili v. Belgium (Grand Chamber)
flags: source is a portal or search page: link the judgment itself
holding_as_summarised: No. Removal would breach Article 3 where there is a real risk of serious, rapid and irreversible decline due to lack of treatment, unless the state assesses that risk.

name: Ponomaryovi v. Bulgaria
flags: source is a portal or search page: link the judgment itself
holding_as_summarised: No. In the circumstances, charging fees on the basis of immigration status breached Article 14 with Article 2 of Protocol No. 1.

name: Popov v. France
flags: source is a portal or search page: link the judgment itself
holding_as_summarised: No, not in these conditions. Holding the children breached Articles 3, 5 and 8, and alternatives to detention had to be considered.

name: Saadi v. the United Kingdom (Grand Chamber)
flags: source is a portal or search page: link the judgment itself
holding_as_summarised: Yes. Short detention to process a claim quickly falls within Article 5(1)(f), provided it is not arbitrary; but the delay in giving reasons breached Article 5(2).

name: V.C.L. and A.N. v. the United Kingdom
flags: source is a portal or search page: link the judgment itself
holding_as_summarised: No, not without first assessing whether they were trafficked. Prosecuting them breached Article 4 and the fairness of the trial under Article 6.

name: Zoletić and Others v. Azerbaijan
flags: source is a portal or search page: link the judgment itself
holding_as_summarised: Yes. Despite credible reports, the authorities did not investigate the alleged forced labour and trafficking, breaching Article 4.

name: Hounga v. Allen
court: Supreme Court of the United Kingdom
holding_as_summarised: No. Public policy against trafficking and in favour of protecting its victims outweighs the illegality defence.

name: Rantsev v. Cyprus and Russia
holding_as_summarised: No. Trafficking falls within Article 4; Cyprus lacked an adequate framework and failed to protect her, and Russia failed to investigate her recruitment.

name: Siliadin v. France
holding_as_summarised: No. Article 4 requires states to make servitude and forced labour criminal offences and enforce them; the law then in force did not give practical and effective protection.

name: Taiwo v. Olaigbe; Onu v. Akwiwu
court: Supreme Court of the United Kingdom
holding_as_summarised: No. Immigration status is not nationality; the discrimination claims failed, although the workers had other remedies.

name: Basfar v. Wong
holding_as_summarised: No. Employing a domestic worker in conditions of forced labour is a “commercial activity” outside diplomatic immunity.

name: Avena and Other Mexican Nationals (Mexico v. United States of America)
holding_as_summarised: Yes. The US breached Article 36 for Mexican nationals sentenced to death and must provide review and reconsideration of their convictions and sentences.

name: Teitiota v. New Zealand
flags: source is a portal or search page: link the judgment itself
holding_as_summarised: No violation on the facts, but the Committee said climate change can trigger the duty not to return people where it exposes them to a real risk to life.

name: Reyes Aguilera, Daniela c/ Estado Nacional
holding_as_summarised: No. The 20-year residence requirement in Decree 432/97 was declared unconstitutional in her case.

name: Social assistance for foreign residents (RE 587.970)
flags: source is a portal or search page: link the judgment itself
holding_as_summarised: Yes. Foreigners resident in Brazil who meet the conditions are entitled to the benefit on the same footing as nationals.

name: Sentencia SU-677/17 (emergency health care for migrants without status)
holding_as_summarised: Yes, at least emergency care, read broadly in light of the right to a dignified life; full enrolment in the health system generally requires regularising status.

name: Health care for Venezuelan migrants (T-210/18)
holding_as_summarised: Yes. Emergency care for undocumented migrants can include treatment for serious illness such as cancer, and the state must help them regularise to join the health system.

name: Sentencia TC/0168/13 (nationality of children of foreign residents)
court: Constitutional Tribunal of the Dominican Republic
flags: source is a portal or search page: link the judgment itself
holding_as_summarised: No. Children of foreigners “in transit”, read to include irregular migrants, are excluded, applied back to 1929; the authorities were ordered to audit civil registries.

name: Expelled Dominicans and Haitians v. Dominican Republic
holding_as_summarised: Yes. The expulsions were arbitrary and collective, and TC/0168/13 and Law 169-14 breached the right to nationality and equality; the State was ordered to leave them without effect.

name: Random migration checks on roads (Amparo en revisión 275/2019)
court: Supreme Court of Justice of Mexico (First Chamber)
holding_as_summarised: No. The migration review provisions breached freedom of movement and led to racial profiling, including of Mexican citizens.

name: 36-hour limit in migration stations (Amparo en revisión 388/2022)
court: Supreme Court of Justice of Mexico (First Chamber)
holding_as_summarised: No more than 36 hours; after that people must continue their migration procedure at liberty.

name: Advisory Opinion OC-16/99 (consular assistance and due process)
holding_as_summarised: Yes. The right to consular information is part of due process; imposing the death penalty without it violates the right not to be arbitrarily deprived of life.

name: Juridical Condition and Rights of Undocumented Migrants (Advisory Opinion OC-18/03)
holding_as_summarised: No. Equality and non-discrimination are peremptory norms; once employed, a migrant holds the labour rights of a worker whatever their status.

name: Advisory Opinion OC-21/14 (children in migration)
holding_as_summarised: States may not detain children for migration reasons; they must find alternatives that keep families together and assess each child’s need for protection.

name: Advisory Opinion OC-25/18 (asylum)
holding_as_summarised: The right to seek and receive asylum and the rule against return to danger bind states; diplomatic asylum is not covered by the American Convention.

name: Pacheco Tineo Family v. Bolivia
holding_as_summarised: Yes. Asylum and expulsion procedures require due process, and the family’s rights, including those of the children, were breached.

name: Roche Azaña v. Nicaragua
holding_as_summarised: Yes. The use of lethal force was unlawful, and the survivor was denied access to justice because he was not told of or included in the proceedings.

name: Vélez Loor v. Panama
holding_as_summarised: Prison sentences to punish irregular migration are incompatible with the American Convention; migrants may be detained only when necessary and proportionate, apart from people held for crimes, with access to consular assistance.

name: Yean and Bosico Girls v. Dominican Republic
holding_as_summarised: No. The refusal was discriminatory and left the girls stateless; a parent’s migratory status cannot be passed on to children.

name: Adam v. Knesset (three-year detention of asylum seekers)
court: Supreme Court of Israel (sitting as High Court of Justice)
holding_as_summarised: No. A nine-judge panel struck down the amendment to the Prevention of Infiltration Law as a disproportionate violation of liberty.

name: Kav LaOved v. Knesset (deposit law)
court: Supreme Court of Israel (sitting as High Court of Justice)
holding_as_summarised: No. The deposit provision was struck down as a disproportionate violation of property rights; withheld money was to be returned.

name: Eitan – Israeli Immigration Policy Center v. Government
court: Supreme Court of Israel (sitting as High Court of Justice)
holding_as_summarised: No. The court struck down both the one-year detention and the open-ended stay at Holot.

name: Galon v. Attorney General (family reunification)
court: Supreme Court of Israel (sitting as High Court of Justice)
holding_as_summarised: Yes, by six to five. The temporary order was upheld on security grounds.

flags: source is a portal or search page: link the judgment itself
